descripcion_es: Proverbs and literary, biblical and historical references that native speakers take for granted.
resumen: Proverbs and allusions (to Shakespeare, the Bible, mythology, history or children's literature) that appear in the press and in speeches without explanation. Understanding them is essential to grasp the tone of a C2-level text.

explicacion.texto: Proverbs are often only half quoted (“Well, when in Rome…”), on the assumption that the listener will complete the rest. Allusions work the same way: saying that something is “a Pyrrhic victory” evokes a whole story in two words.

filas: Don't count your chickens before they're hatched.
Don't treat something as certain before it happens (es: No vendas la piel del oso antes de cazarlo.)
Before an outcome is known.
When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
Follow the customs of the place you are in (es: Donde fueres, haz lo que vieres.)
Adapting to local customs.
Every cloud has a silver lining.
Something good comes out of every bad situation (es: No hay mal que por bien no venga.)
Seeing the good side of something bad.
The proof of the pudding is in the eating.
You can only judge something by trying it (es: Hay que probarlo para juzgarlo; por el fruto se conoce el árbol.)
Judging a reform by its results.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Too many people in charge ruin a task (es: Muchas manos en un plato hacen mucho garabato.)
Committees and lack of coordination.
Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Don't risk everything on a single option (es: No te lo juegues todo a una carta.)
Diversificar riesgos.
Let sleeping dogs lie.
Better not to stir up an old problem (es: Mejor no remover el asunto.)
No reabrir viejos conflictos.
Better safe than sorry.
It is better to take precautions (es: Más vale prevenir que curar.)
Precautionary measures.
A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
Something certain is better than something bigger but uncertain (es: Más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando.)
Accepting a safe offer.
Where there's smoke, there's fire.
Rumours usually have some truth in them (es: Cuando el río suena, agua lleva.)
Rumours and scandals.
Actions speak louder than words.
What people do matters more than what they say (es: Obras son amores, que no buenas razones.)
Judging by deeds.
a Pyrrhic victory
history: a victory that costs more than it is worth
The deal was a Pyrrhic victory for the union.
to cross the Rubicon
history (Caesar): to take an irreversible decision
By calling the referendum, he crossed the Rubicon.
Achilles' heel
mythology: a weak point
Productivity is Spain's Achilles' heel.
to open Pandora's box
mythology: to unleash unforeseen problems
The ruling may open Pandora's box.
a Trojan horse
mythology: a threat disguised as a gift
Critics see the deal as a Trojan horse.
David and Goliath
the Bible: the small against the powerful
A David and Goliath battle against a tech giant.
the writing on the wall
the Bible (Daniel): a sign of an imminent end
The writing was on the wall for the old factory.
a prodigal son
the Bible: someone who comes back after leaving
The prodigal son returned to the club.
to be or not to be
Shakespeare (Hamlet): a fundamental dilemma
To stay or not to stay: that is the question for the UK.
something is rotten in the state of Denmark
Shakespeare (Hamlet): there is hidden corruption
Something is rotten in the state of the club.
Catch-22
Joseph HELLER (1961): a no-win situation caused by contradictory rules
No job without experience, no experience without a job: a Catch-22.
Orwellian / Big Brother
George ORWELL (1949): totalitarian surveillance and manipulation
An Orwellian surveillance system.
Kafkaesque
Franz KAFKA: absurd, oppressive bureaucracy
A Kafkaesque visa process.
a can of worms
informal: a matter that, once opened, brings lots of problems
Reforming the tax code would open a can of worms.

ejemplos.frase: Don't count your chickens: the contract hasn't been signed yet.
ejemplos.traduccion: No vendas la piel del oso: el contrato aún no se ha firmado.

ejemplos.frase: Losing my job was awful, but every cloud has a silver lining: I finally started my own business.
ejemplos.traduccion: Perder el trabajo fue horrible, pero no hay mal que por bien no venga: por fin monté mi propio negocio.

ejemplos.frase: Lack of investment remains the Achilles' heel of the region.
ejemplos.traduccion: La falta de inversión sigue siendo el talón de Aquiles de la región.

ejemplos.frase: Getting a residence permit was a Kafkaesque experience.
ejemplos.traduccion: Conseguir el permiso de residencia fue una experiencia kafkiana.

ejemplos.frase: The small brewery's lawsuit against the multinational was a real David and Goliath story.
ejemplos.traduccion: La demanda de la pequeña cervecera contra la multinacional fue una auténtica historia de David contra Goliat.

ejemplos.frase: When the main sponsor withdrew, the writing was on the wall.
ejemplos.traduccion: Cuando se retiró el patrocinador principal, el final estaba cantado.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: It's the heel of Achilles of the economy.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: It's the Achilles' heel of the economy.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Don't sell the bear's skin before hunting it.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Don't count your chickens before they're hatched.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Proverbs are not translated literally: you look for the equivalent.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: There is no bad that good doesn't come.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Every cloud has a silver lining.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Equivalent of Spanish “no hay mal que por bien no venga”.

ejercicios.frase: Don't count your ___ before they're hatched.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the first proverb in the table, equivalent to Spanish “No vendas la piel del oso antes de cazarlo”: don't treat as achieved something you don't have yet. The clue is “before they're hatched”: what comes out of an egg (hatch) is chicks, “chickens”. Proverbs have a fixed form, so no other word will do. Often only the first half is quoted: “Don't count your chickens”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish: “No vendas la piel del oso antes de cazarlo”.
ejercicios.traduccion: No vendas la piel del oso antes de cazarlo (literalmente: no cuentes tus pollos antes de que salgan del cascarón).

errores_previstos.explicacion: What you count too early is the chickens that will hatch, not the eggs; the fixed proverb says “chickens”.
You need the plural, “chickens”, because it refers to several chicks and agrees with “they're hatched”.
This is a calque of the Spanish proverb about the bear; English uses a different image.

glosario.significado: dar algo por hecho antes de tiempo

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the proverb in the table for “seeing the good side of something bad”, equivalent to Spanish “No hay mal que por bien no venga”. The image is a dark cloud whose edge shines with sunlight: “a silver lining”. The missing word is “lining”, the lining or edge. It is also very common on its own: “the silver lining is that…” (the good thing about all this is that…).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish: “No hay mal que por bien no venga”.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hay mal que por bien no venga (literalmente: toda nube tiene un forro de plata).

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Line” is a line; the fixed expression is “silver lining”, the silver lining or edge.
“The bright side” is a different expression (“look on the bright side”), but the proverb says “silver lining”.

glosario.significado: el lado bueno de algo malo (literalmente, forro de plata)
glosario.definicion_l: a consoling aspect of a difficult situation
any collection of particles (e.g., smoke or dust) or gases that is visible · a visible mass of water or ice particles suspended at a considerable altitude

ejercicios.frase: When in ___, do as the Romans do.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the proverb in the table about adapting to local customs, equivalent to Spanish “Donde fueres, haz lo que vieres”. The clue is in the second half: “as the Romans do” requires the place to be Rome, the city of the Romans. Because it is so well known, it is often only half quoted: “Well, when in Rome…”. It is a proverb with a fixed form and the place cannot be changed.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish: “Donde fueres, haz lo que vieres”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Donde fueres, haz lo que vieres (literalmente: cuando estés en Roma, haz como los romanos).

por_opcion.Rome: Correct: the Romans are the inhabitants of Rome; this is the fixed form of the proverb.
por_opcion.Italy: Incorrect: the proverb does not talk about Italy, and “Romans” are not Italians in general.
por_opcion.doubt: Incorrect here: “When in doubt…” exists as the start of other sentences (“if you are not sure…”), but it does not fit with “do as the Romans do”.
por_opcion.Greece: Incorrect: Greece has nothing to do with the Romans in the proverb.

glosario.significado: donde fueres, haz lo que vieres

glosario.definicion_l: a New Testament book containing an exposition of the doctrines of Saint Paul; written in AD 58

ejercicios.frase: They won the election, but lost so many seats that it was a ___ victory.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the historical allusion “a Pyrrhic victory”, a victory that costs more than it is worth, after King Pyrrhus, who defeated the Romans with enormous losses. The clue is the contrast “They won … but lost so many seats”: they win, but at a disproportionate cost. The adjective is written with a capital letter because it comes from a proper name. Spanish has the same expression, “victoria pírrica”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Pyrrhic victory: it costs more than it is worth.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ganaron las elecciones, pero perdieron tantos escaños que fue una victoria pírrica.

por_opcion.Pyrrhic: Correct: a victory that costs so much that it is almost a defeat.
por_opcion.Trojan: Incorrect: it alludes to the Trojan horse, a threat disguised as a gift; “a Trojan victory” is not an expression.
por_opcion.Kafkaesque: Incorrect: Kafkaesque describes absurd, oppressive bureaucracy, not a costly victory.
por_opcion.prodigal: Incorrect: “prodigal” alludes to the son who comes back after leaving, or to someone who squanders money; it does not fit with victory.

glosario.definicion_l: an area that includes places where several people can sit

ejercicios.frase: Low productivity is the heel of Achilles of our economy.
respuestas: Low productivity is the Achilles' heel of our economy.
Low productivity is the Achilles heel of our economy.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the mythological allusion “Achilles' heel”, a weak point, and the first typical mistake in this unit: Spanish says “el talón de Aquiles”, but English uses the fixed form with the possessive 's, “Achilles' heel”. The clue is the structure “the heel of Achilles”, a calque of the Spanish. The correct form is “the Achilles' heel of our economy”, and it is also acceptable without the apostrophe, “Achilles heel”, which is very common in the press.
ejercicios.traduccion: La baja productividad es el talón de Aquiles de nuestra economía.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Low productivity is the heel of Achilles of our economy.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: “the heel of Achilles” is a calque of the Spanish; the fixed form is “Achilles' heel”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Low productivity is the Achilles' heel from our economy.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The complement goes with “of” (“the Achilles' heel of”), not with “from”.

glosario.definicion_l: a seemingly small but actual mortal weakness
the quality of being productive or having the power to produce · (economics) the ratio of the quantity and quality of units produced to the labor per unit of time

ejercicios.frase: You need experience to get a job, but you need a job to get experience: it's a real ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the literary allusion “Catch-22”, after the novel by Joseph HELLER (1961): a no-win situation created by contradictory rules. The clue is the sentence itself: each condition requires the other, and neither can be met first. It is used as a noun (“a Catch-22”) or as an adjective (“a Catch-22 situation”). In Spanish you would say “la pescadilla que se muerde la cola”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Catch-22”: a no-win situation caused by contradictory rules.
ejercicios.traduccion: Necesitas experiencia para conseguir trabajo, pero necesitas trabajo para conseguir experiencia: es un círculo vicioso sin salida.

por_opcion.Catch-22: Correct: a no-win situation caused by requirements that cancel each other out.
por_opcion.Trojan horse: Incorrect: a Trojan horse is something that looks innocent but hides a threat.
por_opcion.Pandora's box: Incorrect: to open Pandora's box is to unleash unforeseen troubles; it does not describe a vicious circle.
por_opcion.David and Goliath: Incorrect: it describes the fight of the small against the powerful, not contradictory rules.

glosario.significado: situación sin salida, la pescadilla que se muerde la cola

ejercicios.frase: Don't put all your eggs in one ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the proverb in the table about diversifying risk, equivalent to Spanish “No te lo juegues todo a una carta”. The image is a farmer carrying all his eggs in one basket: if he drops it, he loses everything. The fixed word is “basket”. It is very common in economics and finance to talk about diversifying investments or suppliers.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish: “No te lo juegues todo a una carta”.
ejercicios.traduccion: No te lo juegues todo a una carta (literalmente: no pongas todos los huevos en una sola cesta).

errores_previstos.explicacion: The fixed proverb says “basket”; changing the object breaks the expression.
This is a calque of Spanish “a una carta”; the English proverb uses the image of eggs and a basket.

glosario.palabra: to put all your eggs in one basket

glosario.definicion_l: a container that is usually woven and has handles · the quantity contained in a basket

ejercicios.frase: Once he had resigned publicly, he had crossed the ___: there was no way back.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the historical allusion “to cross the Rubicon”: Caesar crossed the river Rubicon with his army, which amounted to a declaration of war with no way back. It means to take an irreversible decision. The clue is in “there was no way back”, which explains the meaning. Spanish has the same expression, “cruzar el Rubicón”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Cross the Rubicon” = to take an irreversible decision.
ejercicios.traduccion: Una vez que dimitió públicamente, había cruzado el Rubicón: no había vuelta atrás.

por_opcion.Rubicon: Correct: the river Caesar crossed; the expression means to take an irreversible decision.
por_opcion.Rhine: Incorrect: the Rhine is a real river, but it is not part of any expression with this meaning.
por_opcion.Thames: Incorrect: the Thames does not have that symbolic value.
por_opcion.Jordan: Incorrect: the Jordan has biblical connotations (baptism, reaching the Promised Land), but “cross the Jordan” does not mean an irreversible decision.

glosario.significado: cruzar el Rubicón, tomar una decisión irreversible

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the proverb (it is better to take precautions).
ejercicios.frase: Take an umbrella: better safe than ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the proverb “Better safe than sorry”, equivalent to Spanish “Más vale prevenir que curar”, which the table links to precautionary measures. The clue is the advice “Take an umbrella”: you take a precaution just in case. The fixed word is “sorry”, which here means regretful: it is better to be safe than to have to regret it. It is a very common phrase in everyday conversation.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Better safe than sorry” = Spanish “más vale prevenir que curar”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Llévate un paraguas: más vale prevenir que curar.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is a calque of Spanish “que curar”; the English proverb contrasts “safe” and “sorry”.
“Sad” means unhappy; the fixed form is “sorry”, regretful for not having taken precautions.

glosario.definicion_l: covering or applying simultaneously to a number of similar items or elements or groups · a lightweight handheld collapsible canopy

ejercicios.frase: The new surveillance law has been described as ___ by civil rights groups.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the literary allusion “Orwellian”, after George ORWELL and his novel “1984” (1949): it evokes totalitarian surveillance and manipulation. The clue is “surveillance law” and “civil rights groups”: excessive state control over citizens is being criticised. The adjective is written with a capital letter because it derives from a proper name. “Big Brother” belongs to the same family.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los grupos de defensa de los derechos civiles han calificado de orwelliana la nueva ley de vigilancia.

por_opcion.Orwellian: Correct: it evokes the totalitarian surveillance described by ORWELL.
por_opcion.Shakespearean: Incorrect: Shakespearean refers to Shakespeare's style or tragic grandeur, not to surveillance.
por_opcion.Pyrrhic: Incorrect: Pyrrhic only applies to victories that come at too high a price.
por_opcion.prodigal: Incorrect: prodigal alludes to someone who comes back after leaving or to someone who squanders money; it does not describe a law.

glosario.significado: orwelliano, propio de un Estado totalitario que lo vigila todo
glosario.definicion_l: of or relating to the works of George Orwell (especially his picture of a future totalitarian state)
close observation of a person or group (usually by the police)
right or rights belonging to a person by reason of citizenship including especially the fundamental freedoms and privileges guaranteed by the 13th and 14th…

ejercicios.frase: A bird in the hand is worth a hundred flying.
respuestas: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
ejercicios.explicacion: This unit stresses that proverbs are not translated word for word: you look for the equivalent. The English proverb that corresponds to Spanish “Más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando” is “A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush”. The clue is “a hundred flying”, a direct calque of Spanish “ciento volando”. You only need to replace that second half with the fixed English form.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The English version is “worth two in the bush”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando (literalmente: un pájaro en la mano vale por dos en el arbusto).

errores_previstos.respuesta: A bird in the hand is worth a hundred flying.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: “a hundred flying” is a calque of the Spanish proverb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: A bird in the hand is worth two flying.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The number is now the one in the English proverb, but the fixed image is “in the bush”, not “flying”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: A bird in the hand is worth a hundred in the bush.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The English proverb says “two”, not “a hundred”.

glosario.palabra: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush
glosario.significado: más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando

glosario.definicion_l: 43rd President of the United States; son of George Herbert Walker Bush (born in 1946)

ejercicios.frase: When the sponsors pulled out, the writing was on the ___ for the festival.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the biblical allusion “the writing is on the wall”, from the Book of Daniel: a hand wrote on the wall of Belshazzar's palace the announcement of his downfall. It means there are clear signs of an imminent end. The clue is “When the sponsors pulled out”: without sponsors the festival is doomed. The fixed word is “wall”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “The writing is on the wall” = the end is imminent.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cuando los patrocinadores se retiraron, el final del festival estaba cantado.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The fixed expression is “on the wall”; any other surface breaks the allusion.
“On paper” means “in theory”, which has nothing to do with an announced end.

glosario.palabra: the writing is on the wall
glosario.significado: el final está cantado, hay señales claras de que algo acabará

glosario.definicion_l: someone who supports or champions something · an advocate who presents a person (as for an award or a degree or an introduction etc.)

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the proverb in the table for rumours and scandals, equivalent to Spanish “Cuando el río suena, agua lleva”: if there are signs, there must be some truth in it. The clue is “there's fire”: the visible sign of fire is “smoke”. It is a fixed form. It is often used in a shortened version: “no smoke without fire”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish: “Cuando el río suena, agua lleva”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cuando el río suena, agua lleva (literalmente: donde hay humo, hay fuego).

por_opcion.smoke: Correct: smoke is the sign of fire; this is the fixed form of the proverb.
por_opcion.heat: Incorrect: heat comes with fire, but it is not the image in the proverb.
por_opcion.light: Incorrect: “light” is not part of this proverb.
por_opcion.water: Incorrect: it recalls the Spanish proverb about the river and the water, but English uses smoke and fire.

glosario.significado: cuando el río suena, agua lleva

glosario.definicion_l: a cloud of fine particles suspended in a gas · a hot vapor containing fine particles of carbon being produced by combustion

ejercicios.frase: Changing the constitution could open Pandora's ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the mythological allusion “to open Pandora's box”: Pandora opened the box that contained all the evils of the world, which escaped beyond recall. It means to unleash unforeseen and uncontrollable problems. The clue is the verb “open”, which always goes with this allusion. The fixed word is “box”, even though in the original myth it was a jar.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Open Pandora's box” = to unleash unforeseen evils.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cambiar la constitución podría abrir la caja de Pandora.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “Open a can of worms” is another expression in this unit with a similar meaning, but the Pandora one says “box”.
“Open the door to” means to make something possible; the mythological allusion is “Pandora's box”.

glosario.significado: abrir la caja de Pandora, desatar males imprevistos

glosario.definicion_l: the constitution written at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787 and subsequently ratified by the original thirteen states

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words of the proverb in order.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the proverb in the table for judging by deeds, equivalent to Spanish “Obras son amores, que no buenas razones”. It has the structure of a normal comparative: subject “Actions” + verb “speak” + comparative “louder” + “than words”. The clue for the order is the capital letter of “Actions”, which starts the sentence, and the pair “louder than”, which always goes together.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish: “Obras son amores, que no buenas razones”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Obras son amores, que no buenas razones (literalmente: los actos hablan más alto que las palabras).

errores_previstos.explicacion: It reverses the meaning: the proverb says that deeds are worth more than words. Also, “Actions” has the capital letter that starts the sentence.
The verb “speak” goes after the subject and before the comparative “louder than”.

glosario.significado: obras son amores, que no buenas razones

glosario.definicion_l: characterized by or producing sound of great volume or intensity · tastelessly showy

descripcion_larga_es: Proverbs and cultural allusions (to the Bible, mythology, history, Shakespeare or Orwell) that the English-language press and speeches take for granted and often only half quote. Understanding them is key to grasping the tone and irony of a C2-level text. Spanish speakers tend to translate their own proverbs word for word, and nobody understands the result.

contexto.que_es: Proverbs are set phrases that carry a lesson (Better safe than sorry), and allusions are brief references to a story everybody knows (a Pyrrhic victory, Achilles' heel, Catch-22). In both cases the form is fixed and the meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words, but from the story or tradition they evoke.
contexto.por_que_importa: Journalists and speakers use them to sum up a complex idea in two words and to add colour or irony. If you don't recognise them, you miss the meaning of a headline or an argument; if you translate them from Spanish, the listener understands nothing or finds it comical. In a high-level exam, using one in the right place shows cultural command, and using one wrongly shows the opposite.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In headlines, opinion columns, political speeches and educated conversation, above all to comment on results, risks or decisions. The signs are a sentence cut off halfway or an unexpected capital letter (Rubicon, Pandora). Spanish speakers should look for the English equivalent of the proverb, not its literal translation: “No vendas la piel del oso” is “Don't count your chickens”.
